title: Recovery — Post-Run Reset
subtitle: Lower-body focused, for after run days
coaching_note: Do this within a couple hours of your run if you can — the tissue is warm and responds better than stretching cold the next day.

phases.name: Stretch
phases.coaching_note: Hold each stretch at least 45 seconds. No bouncing — ease in, breathe, let it release.

exercises.name: Standing Quad Stretch
exercises.form_cue: Hold your ankle behind you, knees together, gentle pull toward your glute. Hold a wall for balance.
exercises.why: Quads absorb a lot of eccentric load on every run stride — they tighten up fast and need this.

exercises.name: Standing Hamstring Stretch (foot elevated)
exercises.form_cue: Heel on a low step or curb, leg straight, hinge forward from the hips, keep your back flat.
exercises.why: Tight hamstrings limit stride length and pull on the pelvis — a common source of lower back tightness after long runs.

exercises.name: Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch
exercises.form_cue: Back knee down, tuck your tailbone under first, then gently drive the hips forward.
exercises.why: The hip flexors shorten with every running stride — this is the single highest-value stretch for a runner.

exercises.name: Figure-4 Glute Stretch
exercises.form_cue: Lying on your back, cross one ankle over the opposite knee, pull the uncrossed thigh toward your chest.
exercises.why: Releases the glute and piriformis — tightness here is a common driver of IT band and knee pain in runners.

exercises.name: Standing Calf Stretch
exercises.form_cue: Heel down, toes up on a wall or step. Straight-knee version for the calf, slight bend for the soleus.
exercises.why: Calves take huge eccentric load at push-off — leaving them tight is a direct path to Achilles and plantar issues.

progression_notes: If one side consistently feels tighter than the other, spend an extra 15-20 seconds there rather than rushing to match the timer.
